name: Topical tobacco paste

lead: Topical tobacco paste is listed by Wikipedia among types of smokeless tobacco, described as a paste applied to the skin and absorbed through the dermis.[1] It is a traditional poultice-style preparation.
No published source documents a skin-appearance effect from it. It is included here because it appears in traditional practice and in smokeless tobacco taxonomies.

paras: It is applied to the skin as a paste. Details of traditional preparations are not well documented.

Smokeless tobacco as a category contains nicotine and carcinogens such as tobacco-specific nitrosamines, and is linked to oral cancer.[2] Wikipedia notes no safe level of smokeless tobacco use is established.[1]

lead: Topical tobacco paste is named by Wikipedia as one type of smokeless tobacco, described as a paste applied to the skin and absorbed through the dermis.[1] A review of smokeless tobacco includes it in a list with chewing tobacco, naswar, snuff, snus and gutka.[2]

No studies describe its effect on appearance. The research that exists concerns smokeless tobacco generally, which contains more than twenty-five carcinogenic compounds including tobacco-specific nitrosamines, cadmium and formaldehyde, and is linked to oral cancer.[2]

paras: Wikipedia's smokeless tobacco article lists topical tobacco paste among product types, as a paste applied to the skin and absorbed through the dermis.[1]

All smokeless tobacco products contain nicotine, and Wikipedia states there is no safe level of use; oral, oesophageal and pancreatic cancers are associated with it.[1] A 2014 review concluded oral cancer risk varies by product type, from very low for moist snuff to higher for dry snuff.[2] These findings concern oral use, and no skin-specific data were located.
